description: Registered, classified differences between the real backend decoders and the Python validator (adapter-contract.md section 8.3/8.4). A difference not listed here fails WireContractParityTest; a listed one that no longer differs also fails. Classes: B existing backend/firmware inconsistency, C simulator parity gap, D intentional legacy compatibility, E unsupported input requiring rejection. Class A (a schema mistake) is never registered.

entries.rationale: A message is exactly one UTF-8 JSON document without a byte-order mark and with unique member names. The backend (Jackson readValue/readTree) tolerates a BOM, trailing content and repeated member names. The validator rejects them because they make a document ambiguous. No real producer sends them; the backend is unchanged in P5.1 and its tolerance is not a promise.

The contract types these members as text. Jackson coerces a JSON number or boolean to text for String members (sensorType, unit, capabilityKey) and the ACK handler reads reason with asText(), so the backend accepts values and lengths the contract does not define. The firmware and the simulator only send text of at most 9 characters. Legacy-v1 consumers keep today's tolerance because the backend is unchanged.

The contract defines identifiers as canonical 8-4-4-4-12 UUID text (java.util.UUID.fromString also accepts 1-1-1-1-1), readbackCommandId as a UUID or absent (Jackson turns an empty string into null) and telemetry timestamps as ISO-8601 instants with an upper-case T and Z/offset (Jackson also accepts a numeric epoch, lower-case designators and surrounding whitespace, because it trims UUID and Instant text). The firmware and the simulator send only the defined forms.

The backend decoder throws instead of rejecting and dropping the message. DeviceCommandAckMessageHandler.parseTimestampOrNull calls Instant.ofEpochSecond for any integral timestamp, so a value outside the Instant range raises DateTimeException, which escapes the handler unacknowledged, so the broker redelivers the same poison message. Recorded, not fixed (the Phase 4 safety semantics are frozen); the validator rejects them with a fixed code. (The telemetry listener's equivalent for the JSON text null was fixed in P5.3 by the extraction into the MQTT adapter's decoder, which rejects it as MALFORMED_JSON, so it no longer differs and is no longer registered.)

CommandValueValidator.requireWholeNumber ends with number.intValue(), which narrows a 64-bit integer to 32 bits before the 0..180 range check, so the SERVO value 4294967386 (2^32 + 90) is accepted as angle 90. The validator compares the unnarrowed number and rejects it. Recorded, not fixed in P5.1.

The MQTT path treats contractVersion and requires as ordinary unknown fields, exactly as the committed listener and handlers always did, so a message declaring major 2.0, a malformed version text or a non-empty requires list is accepted and processed as a legacy-v1 message. The contract forbids this (section 6 resolution table: reject permanently, never reinterpret), and the HTTP adapter, the Python validator and the SDKs do reject it. It is registered, not tightened, because section 6.1 rule 6 and the Phase 4 freeze say a historically accepted payload is never rejected more strictly in this phase, and no shipped producer (the firmware, the simulator, the SDKs on MQTT) declares a version the backend does not know. Consequence to remember: a future producer that relies on requires to make a receiver refuse a message it cannot honour is NOT protected over MQTT until the MQTT decoder resolves versions (a decision for the owner, with a migration note for existing devices).

simulatorEntries.rationale: Since P5.5 the simulator applies the firmware's freshness rule (absolute 30 s, whole-second clock) and requires a JSON integer timestamp, so the former class C differences are gone. One difference is kept on purpose: the simulator accepts any non-empty string as commandId, because its existing tests and tools use short ids, and the backend always sends UUIDs, so nothing real depends on it. The firmware, the SDK and the validator require canonical UUID text.
